hints: Recall the order of the electromagnetic spectrum by wavelength and locate $8.4 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}$ relative to visible light ($\sim 4$ to $7 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}$).
teacher_walkthrough: The electromagnetic spectrum is ordered by wavelength. Visible light spans approximately $4.0 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}$ to $7.0 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}$.
The given wavelength is $$\lambda = 8.4 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m} = 8400 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m}$$ which is longer than red light but shorter than microwaves ($\sim 10^{-2} \text{ m}$).
This region is the infra-red region.
common_pitfalls: Confusing $10^{-6} \text{ m}$ with ultraviolet; ultraviolet has shorter wavelength than visible, not longer.
Stating thermal radiation or heat radiation instead of the principal named region infra-red.

hints: Recall the universal wave equation for electromagnetic waves in vacuum with speed $c = 3.0 \times 10^8 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
Set up $f = c/\lambda$ and convert the final frequency in Hz to THz using $1 \text{ THz} = 10^{12} \text{ Hz}$.
teacher_walkthrough: All electromagnetic waves in vacuum travel at $$c = 3.0 \times 10^8 \text{ m s}^{-1}$$ governed by $$c = f\lambda$$
Rearrange for frequency: $$f = \frac{c}{\lambda}$$
Substitute values: $$f = \frac{3.0 \times 10^8}{8.4 \times 10^{-6}}$$
Evaluate: $$f = 0.3571 \times 10^{14} \text{ Hz} = 3.57 \times 10^{13} \text{ Hz}$$
Convert to THz: $$f = \frac{3.57 \times 10^{13}}{10^{12}} = 35.7 \text{ THz} \approx 36 \text{ THz}$$
common_pitfalls: Using incorrect power of ten for THz and giving $3.6 \times 10^{13} \text{ THz}$ by omitting division by $10^{12}$.
Rounding too early or using $c = 3 \times 10^8$ incorrectly in denominator, leading to inverted calculation $f = \lambda/c$.

hints: Recall the condition for stable interference in terms of how the phase relationship between the two waves varies with time.
teacher_walkthrough: Coherence is the condition for a stable, observable interference pattern.
Two waves are coherent when they have a constant phase difference with time, which for light of the same frequency means the same frequency and waveform.
walkthrough: B1 for constant phase difference (between the waves) (with time).
common_pitfalls: Stating same amplitude or same speed instead of constant phase difference; coherence is about phase, not intensity.
Stating in phase rather than constant phase difference; coherent waves can have any constant phase difference, not necessarily zero.

hints: Read Fig. 5.2 carefully: 22 mm covers 8 fringe spacings, so first determine a single fringe spacing $x$ in metres.
Recall the double-slit equation $x = \lambda D / a$ and rearrange to make slit separation $a$ the subject.
Substitute $\lambda = 6.2 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}$, $D = 2.8 \text{ m}$ and your value of $x$, keeping all distances in metres.
teacher_walkthrough: The double-slit fringe spacing is governed by $$x = \frac{\lambda D}{a}$$ where $x$ is adjacent bright fringe separation, $D$ is slit to screen distance and $a$ is slit separation.
First find $x$ from the 8-fringe width: $$x = \frac{22 \times 10^{-3}}{8}$$
Rearrange for $a$: $$a = \frac{\lambda D}{x}$$
Substitute: $$a = \frac{(6.2 \times 10^{-7}) \times 2.8}{2.75 \times 10^{-3}}$$
Evaluate numerator: $$(6.2 \times 10^{-7}) \times 2.8 = 17.36 \times 10^{-7} = 1.736 \times 10^{-6}$$
walkthrough: C1 for use of $a = \lambda D / x$.
common_pitfalls: Using 22 mm directly as $x$ instead of dividing by 8, giving a slit separation 8 times too small.
Leaving $x$ in mm ($2.75 \text{ mm}$) while $\lambda$ and $D$ are in metres, causing a $10^3$ error.

hints: Recall the path difference condition for the first dark fringe measured from the central maximum.
teacher_walkthrough: Destructive interference forming a dark fringe requires waves to arrive in antiphase.
For the nearest dark fringe to the central maximum, the condition is $$\text{path difference} = \frac{\lambda}{2}$$
Substitute $\lambda = 6.2 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}$: $$\text{path difference} = \frac{6.2 \times 10^{-7}}{2} = 3.1 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}$$
common_pitfalls: Giving path difference as one full wavelength $\lambda$; that is the condition for the next bright fringe, not the first dark fringe.
Giving path difference as zero because P is central maximum; Q is displaced so the two paths are no longer equal.

hints: Recall the phase difference corresponding to constructive interference at a bright fringe other than the central fringe.
teacher_walkthrough: Bright fringes correspond to constructive interference where waves arrive in phase.
At the central fringe P the path difference is zero and phase difference is zero.
At the next bright fringe R the path difference is one full wavelength $\lambda$, which corresponds to a phase difference of one full cycle: $$360^{\circ} \text{ or } 2\pi \text{ rad}$$
common_pitfalls: Giving $180^{\circ}$ or $\pi \text{ rad}$; that is the dark fringe condition at Q, not the bright fringe at R.
Confusing path difference with phase difference and answering with a distance such as $6.2 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}$.
